questions.question: How do register, handleSubmit, and formState.errors work in React Hook Form?
questions.title: React Hook Form Registration, Validation, and Errors
questions.direct_answer: `register` connects a named native field to React Hook Form and can attach validation rules. `handleSubmit` runs those rules and calls the valid or invalid callback with the result. `formState.errors` contains field-specific failures that the component can render. Together they connect input collection, validation, and submission without manually storing every value in component state.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the core APIs are connected as one data and validation flow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing method names without explaining the ref, handlers, callbacks, and errors.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect typed registration to accessible feedback and server revalidation.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Spread the registration result onto a compatible native input.
`handleSubmit(onValid, onInvalid?)` validates before calling either callback.
`formState.errors.fieldName` holds that field’s current validation error.
Type `useForm<FormValues>()` so field names and submitted data agree.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
React Hook Form manages a form around registered fields. Calling `register("email")` returns the field name, a ref, and change and blur handlers. Spreading those props onto a native input lets the library observe the field without creating a separate React state variable for every keystroke.

Validation rules can be supplied at registration. For example, an email can be required and checked against a pattern. When the form is submitted, `handleSubmit` gathers the registered values and runs the configured validation. It calls the first callback only when the client-side rules pass, and it can call an optional second callback when they fail.

The failures appear in `formState.errors` under the same typed field names. A component can render `errors.email?.message` next to the email input and connect it with `aria-describedby` so the message is useful visually and to assistive technology.

These rules improve feedback, but they are not a security boundary. The server must validate the submitted values again because browser code can be bypassed. Server failures can be shown as field or root errors after the request returns.

The three APIs form one path: register the field, validate and collect it through `handleSubmit`, then render any failures from `formState.errors`. Keeping the form value type as the shared contract makes that path easier to change safely.

sections.title: Each API has one job in the submission path
sections.content: Registration describes how a field participates, submission decides whether collected values are valid, and form state exposes the result to the UI. The returned registration props should stay together; dropping the ref or handler can break tracking even though the input still renders.

sections.title: Registration turns DOM events into typed form data
sections.content:
For a native field, `register` returns the connection points React Hook Form needs: a stable name, a ref to the element, and handlers for changes and blur. Its options can express required, length, numeric, pattern, or custom validation. Options such as `valueAsNumber` transform a browser string before validation and submission, which keeps the TypeScript form type honest.

`handleSubmit` returns an event handler suitable for the form’s `onSubmit`. It prevents the normal unchecked handoff, reads the registered values, runs validation, and then selects `onValid` or `onInvalid`. The valid callback may be asynchronous. Request failures still need deliberate handling because passing client validation does not guarantee that a network request or server rule will succeed.

`formState` is subscription-based state for the form. Reading `errors.email` causes the component to respond when that part changes. Error messages should describe how to fix the value, and the input should expose `aria-invalid` plus a relationship to its message. This makes validation a visible state of the field rather than a detached alert after submission.

sections.title: From a registered field to either submitted data or an error
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[register name and rules] --> B[input ref and events]
  B --> C[handleSubmit collects values]
  C --> D{client rules pass?}
  D -->|Yes| E[onValid receives typed data]
  D -->|No| F[onInvalid receives errors]
  F --> G[formState.errors renders feedback]
  E --> H[server validates again]
```

questions.question: When should you use Controller in React Hook Form?
questions.title: Using Controller at Controlled Component Boundaries
questions.direct_answer: Use `Controller` when a component is controlled and cannot accept React Hook Form’s normal `ref`, `name`, `onChange`, and `onBlur` registration props directly. Its render function supplies `value`, `onChange`, `onBlur`, `name`, and `ref` to adapt a date picker, rating widget, or UI-library input. Native inputs should normally use `register` instead.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether Controller is understood as an adapter rather than a default wrapper.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Double-registering the widget or leaving its controlled value undefined.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain value-shape transformation and ref forwarding at the boundary.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `register` first for native or ref-friendly inputs.
Use `Controller` for externally controlled components with a `value` API.
Pass the supplied `field` value and handlers to the component’s matching props.
Provide a defined default value; do not use `undefined` as the controlled default.
Do not spread `register` onto a field already managed by `Controller`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`Controller` is an adapter between React Hook Form and a controlled component. A native input usually works with `register` because it exposes a DOM ref and familiar event props. A date picker, autocomplete, slider, or design-system widget may instead require an explicit `value` and report changes through a custom callback.

The `Controller` render function provides a `field` object containing `value`, `onChange`, `onBlur`, `name`, and `ref`. The application maps those pieces to the component’s API. For example, a rating widget can receive `field.value` as its selected score and call `field.onChange(nextScore)` when a star is selected.

The field needs a stable initial value through `defaultValues` or `defaultValue`. Using `undefined` creates the same ownership ambiguity as any controlled React input. Validation rules can be placed on `Controller`, and `fieldState.error` can be rendered beside that specific widget.

A frequent mistake is double registration: using `Controller` and also spreading `register` on the rendered input. That creates two competing connections. Another boundary is transformation; if a widget emits an object but the form should store an ID, the adapter should intentionally pass the ID to `field.onChange`.

I use `Controller` only at this integration boundary. Native fields stay simpler with `register`, while components whose value must be driven through props get one explicit adapter.

sections.title: Controller translates between two component contracts
sections.content: React Hook Form expects a name, current value, update signal, blur signal, and focusable ref. A controlled widget may expose those ideas under different prop names or may emit a different value shape. `Controller` creates one place to translate without making the whole form manually controlled.

sections.title: Map value, events, focus, and validation deliberately
sections.content:
The render callback receives both `field` and `fieldState`. `field.value` is the current form value. `field.onChange` reports the widget’s next value, while `field.onBlur` marks the interaction boundary. Passing `field.ref` to the actual focusable element lets React Hook Form focus the field after a validation failure. `fieldState.error` belongs to that field and can drive its accessible message.

Not every widget reports a DOM event. A select library may call `onChange(option)`; a date picker may return a date or `null`. The adapter chooses what the form stores: the full object, an ID, or a formatted value. That transformation must agree with the form’s TypeScript type and server payload instead of relying on a cast later.

Default values define the comparison baseline for dirty state and keep the widget controlled from its first render. Prefer form-level `defaultValues` when several fields share the same initialization. Reserve `Controller` for components that need it because adding it around an ordinary input creates more code without adding a useful boundary.

sections.title: Controller is a two-way adapter, not a second registration
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[React Hook Form state] -->|field.value| B[Controller adapter]
  B -->|component value prop| C[controlled widget]
  C -->|custom change callback| B
  B -->|field.onChange next value| A
  D[field rules] --> A
  A --> E[fieldState.error]
  E --> F[accessible error message]
```

questions.question: How do you validate and submit a React Hook Form safely?
questions.title: Safe Validation and Submission with React Hook Form
questions.direct_answer: Define field rules for fast client feedback, submit through `handleSubmit`, show messages from `formState.errors`, and use `isSubmitting` to prevent accidental repeat actions. In the async submit callback, handle request failures and map server validation to `setError`. The server must still validate, authorize, and safely process every value because browser validation can be bypassed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether client feedback, async state, and server trust are separated.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating passed client validation as security or ignoring request failures.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map server errors back to fields and address duplicate submissions.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Client rules improve feedback; server rules enforce trust and business constraints.
`handleSubmit` calls the valid callback only after configured client validation passes.
Use typed conversions such as `valueAsNumber` before validating numeric data.
Catch request failures and expose field or root messages with `setError`.
Disable duplicate submission with `formState.isSubmitting`, not a permanent flag.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A safe form has two validation boundaries. React Hook Form provides the browser boundary: field rules produce immediate, specific feedback and `handleSubmit` calls the submit callback only when those rules pass. The server is the trust boundary because a request can be changed or sent without the React application.

I define a typed form value and transform browser strings where needed. For example, `valueAsNumber` makes an age a number before a minimum-age rule runs. Error messages come from `formState.errors` and are connected to their fields, so users can correct the exact value that failed.

The submit callback is usually asynchronous. While it runs, `isSubmitting` can disable the submit button and change its label, which prevents common repeat clicks. The request is wrapped in error handling because network failures and server rejections are different from client validation failures.

For example, if the server says an email is already registered, `setError("email", ...)` places that message beside the email. A general service failure belongs in a root error. The server still repeats format and business validation, checks authorization, and protects duplicate writes where the operation requires it.

This produces one clear flow: useful client feedback, one guarded request, authoritative server validation, and server errors returned to the relevant place in the form.

sections.title: Feedback and trust belong at different boundaries
sections.content: Browser validation helps the person complete the form; it cannot prove that a request is honest. Treat the typed client data as a convenient payload, not as trusted data. A robust submit path represents validation, pending, success, and failure instead of assuming that a valid-looking form guarantees a successful request.

sections.title: Model submission as a small state machine
sections.content:
Before submission, registration rules can validate required values, ranges, patterns, and custom relationships. Conversion should happen before a rule that depends on the target type. Without `valueAsNumber`, a number input still begins as browser text. Messages should remain concrete and stable so the learner can see which rule failed and what correction is possible.

`handleSubmit` separates invalid form data from the valid callback, but an accepted callback can still fail. Await the request and handle expected server responses. Use `setError` for field-specific rejections and a root error for failures without one field owner. Do not turn every server failure into a successful state by silently ignoring the exception.

Pending UI should follow `isSubmitting` so it is reset by the form lifecycle. The backend must repeat validation, enforce authorization, and consider idempotency for operations that must not be duplicated. After success, reset or navigate only when the product flow calls for it; preserving values may be more helpful when the request fails.

sections.title: Client feedback leads to an authoritative server decision
sections.content:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant F as React Hook Form
  participant S as Server
  U->>F: submit registered fields
  F->>F: convert and validate client rules
  alt client rules fail
    F-->>U: field errors
  else client rules pass
    F->>S: typed request payload
    S->>S: validate and authorize again
    alt server accepts
      S-->>F: success
      F-->>U: completion state
    else server rejects
      S-->>F: field or general error
      F-->>U: setError feedback
    end
  end
```
